title: How our pipelines compare to community conventions
text: The Snakemake community has a recommended way to lay out a workflow, and the Snakemake workflow catalog lists workflows that follow it. The lab’s three pipelines follow a different pattern, inherited from the PhanstielLab pipelines (dietJuicer, bagPipes). Neither is wrong. This page puts them side by side so that when you read a catalog workflow, or someone reads ours, nothing is a surprise, and so you know which of our habits are deliberate and which are just history.

section: What we do differently, and why
text:
What we do differently, and why

workflows/*.snakefile instead of workflow/Snakefile
MicroCPipe has two workflows (core and merge) in one repository, so it needs two names, and the launchers always pass -s. The cost is small but real: snakemake -n in the repository root does nothing useful, editors do not recognize .snakefile as Snakemake without a setting, and the catalog’s tools look for workflow/Snakefile. Renaming the folder to workflow/ and the main file to Snakefile (keeping merge.smk or a second Snakefile beside it) would cost one line in each launcher. Low priority.


Profiles in the repository
The catalog treats the cluster as the user’s business. The lab ships one profile per cluster because the people running the pipelines move between a few known clusters, and a profile that already has the right partition names saves each of them a day. The launchers pick the profile from --profile, then $<NAME>_PROFILE, then hpcProfile in the config, so the repository stays neutral and each person sets their cluster once in ~/.bashrc. Keep this. Two things to fix:

Shipped profiles should not contain real account names. MicroCPipe and TTpipe use <account> placeholders and MicroCPipe’s launcher refuses to start until they are filled in; ChromSimPipe’s longleaf and pioneer profiles carry real accounts.
Snakemake 8 automatically uses profiles/default/ (relative to the current directory, then to the Snakefile) as a workflow profile. The lab’s profiles/ folder is exactly where Snakemake looks, so never name a site profile default unless you mean that.



Resources only in profiles
Rules declare threads: and nothing else; set-threads and set-resources in each profile give every rule its CPUs, memory and time. This is the dietJuicer pattern, and it is a good one: moving to a new cluster never touches a rule, and the numbers sit next to the partition names they depend on.
The problem is duplication. MicroCPipe’s five profiles repeat the same 16 set-threads lines and the same set-resources block, and TTpipe’s repeat 24 rules. Add a rule and you edit five files; forget one and that rule silently gets default-resources on that cluster. This has already happened: TTpipe’s eight spike-in rules appear in none of its profiles. The threads: in each rule is also overridden by every profile, so the same number lives in six places.
Snakemake 8 has a direct fix. It reads two profiles: the general one (--profile) and a workflow profile (--workflow-profile, default profiles/default/). Settings in the workflow profile override the general one. So:

profiles/default/config.yaml: set-threads and set-resources for every rule, once.
profiles/<site>/config.yaml: executor, jobs, latency-wait, default-resources with the account and partition, and the GPU partition for the one rule that needs it.

A site that needs a bigger number for one rule (a cluster with large-memory nodes) can still pass --set-resources hic:mem_mb=200000 from its launcher call or keep its own override. This keeps the lab’s idea (no resources in rules) and removes the copies.


A launcher script
Catalog workflows are started with snakemake directly. The lab’s launchers do four things a bare command does not: they are themselves a small SLURM job (#SBATCH -t 10-00:00:00), so the Snakemake process survives you logging out; they pick the site profile; they create the Snakemake venv if needed; and they always add --rerun-incomplete --keep-going -p and the SLURM log directory. For people who run one pipeline a few times a year, that is worth a lot. Keep it.
The cost is that the three launchers are copies of one idea, and they have drifted:

TTpipe.sh
ChromSimPipe.sh

MicroCPipe’s version is the most careful. Bringing the other two up to it is the cheapest improvement on this page.


Snakemake from pip, in a venv
The catalog’s instructions install Snakemake with conda or mamba. The lab installs it with pip (snakemake==8.27.1 in config/requirements.txt) into a venv the launcher builds. The reason is in the profiles’ env.sh files: the conda modules on the lab’s clusters are older than Snakemake 8.27 accepts, so each person installs Miniforge for the per-rule environments anyway, and keeping Snakemake itself out of conda means one less environment to solve. Pinning the exact Snakemake version in a text file is also easy to read. Keep it, with two notes: the SLURM executor plugin is not pinned (>=1.0 in two repositories, unpinned in ChromSimPipe), and the launcher runs pip install on every start, which needs network access on the node the launcher runs on.


Hand-written validation instead of schemas
Catalog workflows call validate(config, "schemas/config.schema.yaml") and validate(samples, "schemas/samples.schema.yaml"). A JSON schema checks types, required keys and allowed values, and can fill in defaults. The lab’s pipelines check the config and samplesheet in Python at parse time instead (TTpipe’s common.smk and ChromSimPipe’s parameters.py have dozens of checks). Those checks do things a schema cannot, such as “reference_condition must be a Condition in the samplesheet” or “the GTF and the genome use the same chromosome naming”, and their messages say how to fix the problem. A schema would still help with the simple cases and would document every key in one file. Use both: a schema for types and allowed values, Python for the checks that compare one input with another.


No wrappers
Snakemake wrappers are tested, versioned snippets for common tools (wrapper: "v3.x.x/bio/samtools/sort"). The lab writes the shell commands itself, with pinned tools in envs/*.yml. For pipelines like MicroCPipe, where the exact flags are the method (bwa mem -5SP -T0, the pairtools options), a visible shell command is easier to review and cite than a wrapper call. Fine as is.


Own HTML reports instead of report()
Snakemake’s report() flag marks outputs for snakemake --report report.html, which bundles them with run statistics and the workflow graph. The lab writes its own static dashboards (qc_report.py in MicroCPipe and TTpipe) with thresholds from the config. Those do more than --report would. Snakemake’s between-workflow cache (cache: True on a rule, with --cache) is a different feature that would suit expensive reference steps, such as TTpipe’s star_index, if several projects share one index. Not needed today.


include: with a hook instead of module
MicroCPipe’s formats.smk is included by two Snakefiles, each defining get_pairs() first (see MicroCPipe). Snakemake’s module system (module formats: snakefile: ... then use rule cool from formats with: input: ...) does the same with an explicit interface, and also lets another lab reuse our rules without copying them. For two Snakefiles in one repository, include: is simpler to read. Switch only if the format rules start being reused across repositories.

How to read this:

“Absolute path” and “path composition” are one issue, and mostly a false alarm. Rules write OUT + "/{group}/logs/...". The linter sees a string that starts with / and calls it absolute; it also dislikes building paths with +. OUT comes from the config, so nothing is really hard-coded. ChromSimPipe writes the same paths as f-strings (f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/...") and gets neither lint. Switching to f-strings would remove 412 of the 444 findings across the three pipelines and make the rest easy to see.
Shell variables from outside the rule ({PY}, {SCRIPTS} in TTpipe) work, because Snakemake fills shell placeholders from global variables too, but a reader cannot see them in the rule. Pass them as params:. MicroCPipe’s three are {workflow.basedir}, which is Snakemake’s own object; that one is a false alarm.
Hardcoded param prefixes are params like outdir = OUT + "/qc/fastqc" that repeat part of an output path. If the output moves, the param does not. Deriving it from the output (lambda w, output: os.path.dirname(output.zip)) keeps them in step.
No log: TTpipe’s sample_table (also the only run: block) and MicroCPipe’s benchmark_summary. Both are fair and both are small.
envvars: is half right for ChromSimPipe: the Snakefile sets CHROMSIM_CONFIG rather than reading it, so asserting it would not help. The lint does point at something real, though: the scripts depend on environment variables that Snakemake does not track.

The linter does not catch the things that matter most in these pipelines, such as the stale-samplesheet bug TTpipe fixed or ChromSimPipe’s parameters that Snakemake cannot see. Run it anyway: once the false alarms are gone, it is a cheap CI step that catches new habits creeping in.

title: How our pipelines compare to community conventions
text:
Tests: dry runs versus .test/
Catalog workflows usually ship a .test/ folder with a few thousand real reads and run the whole workflow in CI. MicroCPipe and TTpipe instead run snakemake -n against placeholder files and assert job counts (see TTpipe). Dry runs are fast, need no conda environments, and are very good at catching broken wiring, switches that pull in the wrong rules, and samplesheet parsing. They cannot catch a wrong flag or a tool that crashes. A small real-data run catches those, but takes minutes and needs the environments. The two are complements. For ChromSimPipe, which has neither, a dry-run fixture is the first thing to add; a real run in CI is not possible without a GPU.

What is worth changing, in order

Bring TTpipe’s and ChromSimPipe’s launchers up to MicroCPipe’s (no venv activation, placeholder check, env.sh check) and add cores: 100 where rules use threads:.

Write paths as f-strings and add snakemake --lint to CI.
Add JSON schemas for the configs and samplesheets, keeping the cross-checks in Python.
Rename workflows/ to workflow/ if the pipelines ever go into the catalog.

Everything else on this page (launchers, profiles in the repository, pip-installed Snakemake, own reports, shell commands instead of wrappers, outputs under one folder) is a deliberate choice that suits how the lab works.

title: ChromSimPipe
text:
ChromSimPipe is the odd one out. It does not process sequencing reads; it runs physics simulations on GPUs and compares them with Hi-C. That makes it the best place to see module 7: outputs that are not single files, scatter-gather, and GPU resources.
Code on this page is pulled from the repository at the pinned commit (e32dd36), and each block links to the same lines on GitHub. Line numbers in the text are the file’s own line numbers.

title: ChromSimPipe
text:
What the pipeline does
Cohesin folds chromosomes by loop extrusion: a cohesin ring loads on chromatin and reels DNA into a growing loop until it falls off or stalls at a CTCF site whose motif points the right way. Where cohesin stalls, and how long it stays, shapes the contact map you measure with Hi-C. ChromSimPipe turns that idea into a test. It takes CTCF peaks (CUT&Tag or ChIP-seq) and a Hi-C map, orients each CTCF site by scanning for the CTCF motif (JASPAR MA0139.1) with FIMO, and simulates a polymer with loop-extruding cohesins (the Hansen lab’s polysim, on polychrom and OpenMM) over a genomic window.
Each condition in the config is one hypothesis: a set of cohesin parameters (lifetime, spacing, stall probability at CTCF) plus a set of CTCF sites. The shipped example has three conditions that ask whether the CTCF sites of a second state, alone or with weaker stalling, explain that state’s Hi-C. For each condition the pipeline turns simulated conformations into a contact map and compares it with the experimental map (contact probability versus distance, loop pileups, insulation).

If there is no graph above, or only a MissingInputException, that is the honest answer: Snakemake builds the graph from the job graph, the job graph needs the input files, and data/ is empty in the repository (each cluster links its own files into it). In text, the order is the one in the header of the Snakefile:



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

# ==============================================================================
# ChromSimPipe - cohesin loop-extrusion simulation workflow (polysim model)
#
# Run with:  sbatch ChromSimPipe.sh
#
# All inputs come from the config file (config/ChromSimConfig.yaml) and the
# samplesheet it names. configs/parameters.py parses both; this file only
# wires the rules together. Every locus in the config's `loci:` list is
# simulated and analysed separately, in <outputDir>/loci/<locus>/.
#
#   Rules, in order:
#     convertHic        per Hi-C sample (shared by all loci)
#     getMotif          once
#     preparePolysim    once (builds polysim's Cython LEF model)
#     orientCTCF        per locus x CTCF sample
#     validateCTCF      per locus
#     simulateShard     per locus x condition x replicate x shard (GPU)
#     mergeShards       per locus x condition x replicate
#     analyzeCondition  per locus x condition (needs convertHic output)
#     benchmarkSummary  once
# ==============================================================================


ChromSimPipe, lines 4-24 view on GitHub


convertHic, getMotif and preparePolysim run once and are shared by every locus. orientCTCF and validateCTCF run per locus. Then the simulation fans out four ways (locus × condition × replicate × shard), mergeShards gathers the shards of each replicate, analyzeCondition gathers the replicates of each condition, and benchmarkSummary collects the timings.
With the shipped config (one locus, three conditions, n_replicates: 3, n_shards: 2) that is 18 simulateShard jobs, 9 mergeShards and 3 analyzeCondition.  The test config (one condition, one replicate, one shard) is the “10-job smoke test” the code guide recommends running first on a new cluster.

title: ChromSimPipe
section: A walk from inputs to outputs
text:
A walk from inputs to outputs

ChromSimSamplesheet.txt: one row per experimental sample, with a CTCF_Peaks path and a Hi-C path (or NA) and free metadata columns. fileNamesFrom: ['Condition'] names each sample.
config/ChromSimConfig.yaml: loci, conditions, physics (polysim:), motif settings, conda environments, job counts (n_replicates, n_shards), outputDir.
configs/parameters.py reads both and exposes everything as Python names.
convertHic converts each needed Hi-C map to .cool at the simulation resolution.
getMotif downloads the motif (only if no local MEME file is given); orientCTCF writes oriented CTCF sites per locus and CTCF sample; validateCTCF checks them.
simulateShard runs one polysim simulation on one GPU and writes HDF5 files of conformations into a shard folder.
mergeShards concatenates the shards of one replicate.
analyzeCondition computes contact maps and comparisons into output/loci/<locus>/analysis/<condition>/.

title: ChromSimPipe
text:
Concepts in the wild

Sentinel .done files, and why



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

rule simulateShard:
    input:
        validated = f"{L('done')}/validateCTCF.done",
        polysim   = rules.preparePolysim.output.done,
        bed       = lambda wildcards: rel(ctcf_bed_path(
            wildcards.locus, COND_LOOKUP[wildcards.condition]["ctcf_type"])),
        ## peak files for the condition's sticky / loading / pausing options (none by default)
        features  = lambda wildcards: [rel(f) for f in
                                       condition_peak_files(COND_LOOKUP[wildcards.condition]).values()]
    output:
        done = f"{L('done')}/simulateShard_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}_shard{{shard}}.done"
    log:
        err = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/simulateShard_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}_shard{{shard}}.err",
        out = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/simulateShard_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}_shard{{shard}}.out"
    benchmark:
        f"{BENCH_DIR}/simulateShard_{{locus}}_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}_shard{{shard}}.tsv"
    params:
        configfile = CONFIGFILE,
        sim_dir    = lambda wildcards: LP(wildcards, "sims"),
        n_shards   = N_SHARDS
    conda: ENV_SIM
    shell:
        """
        CHROMSIM_CONFIG={params.configfile} CHROMSIM_LOCUS={wildcards.locus} \
            "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python" scripts/run_simulation_shard.py \
            --condition {wildcards.condition} \
            --replicate {wildcards.rep} \
            --shard-index {wildcards.shard} \
            --n-shards {params.n_shards} \
            --gpu 0 \
            --output {params.sim_dir} 1> {log.out} 2> {log.err}
        touch {output.done}
        """


ChromSimPipe, lines 280-312 view on GitHub


The only declared output is simulateShard_{condition}_rep{rep}_shard{shard}.done. The real result is a folder of HDF5 files under sims/, and the rule never names it: the script builds the folder name itself, from the condition’s params_name and ctcf_type and the replicate and shard numbers (<params_name>_ctcf-<ctcf_type>_rep<N>_shard<S>/). Snakemake cannot track a path it is never told. So the last line of the shell block, touch {output.done}, marks success. Because Snakemake runs the block in strict mode, a crashed simulation stops before the touch, no marker appears, and the job counts as failed.
Every downstream rule depends on markers, not data:



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

rule mergeShards:
    input:
        lambda wildcards: expand(rules.simulateShard.output.done, locus=wildcards.locus,
                                 condition=wildcards.condition, rep=wildcards.rep,
                                 shard=range(N_SHARDS))
    output:
        done = f"{L('done')}/mergeShards_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}.done"
    log:
        err = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/mergeShards_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}.err",
        out = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/mergeShards_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}.out"
    benchmark:
        f"{BENCH_DIR}/mergeShards_{{locus}}_{{condition}}_rep{{rep}}.tsv"
    params:
        configfile = CONFIGFILE,
        sim_dir    = lambda wildcards: LP(wildcards, "sims"),
        n_shards   = N_SHARDS
    conda: ENV_SIM
    shell:
        """
        CHROMSIM_CONFIG={params.configfile} CHROMSIM_LOCUS={wildcards.locus} \
            "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python" scripts/merge_shards.py \
            --condition {wildcards.condition} \
            --replicate {wildcards.rep} \
            --n-shards {params.n_shards} \
            --results-dir {params.sim_dir} 1> {log.out} 2> {log.err}
        touch {output.done}
        """


ChromSimPipe, lines 315-341 view on GitHub


This is the gather half of a scatter-gather (module 7). The input is one marker per shard of this replicate. rules.simulateShard.output.done is the pattern with {locus}, {condition}, {rep} and {shard} still in it, and expand() fills all four: three from the job’s own wildcards and shard from range(N_SHARDS).
What markers cost you, compared with directory() outputs:

Snakemake does not delete a stale shard folder before rerunning a job, as it would for a declared directory() output. A rerun writes into whatever is there.
Snakemake cannot tell whether the folder still exists. Delete sims/ by hand and the markers still say everything is done. The troubleshooting notes in the repository say exactly this: if the merged folder is missing, delete its .done marker and resubmit.
--summary and --list-changes describe the markers, not the data.

What they buy: the scripts own their folder layout, and adding a new analysis output to run_analysis_all.py needs no change to the workflow (the code guide says so in “Adding new analysis”).
preparePolysim uses a marker for a different reason:



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

## polysim builds its Cython LEF model (LEF_Dynamics.pyx) with pyximport on
## first import. Do that once here, so parallel shards load the built module
## instead of compiling it at the same time.
rule preparePolysim:
    output:
        done = f"{OUT}/done/preparePolysim.done"
    log:
        err = f"{LOG_DIR}/preparePolysim.err"
    conda: ENV_SIM
    shell:
        """
        "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python" -c "import polysim.extrusion, polysim.sim3d" 2> {log.err}
        touch {output.done}
        """


ChromSimPipe, lines 207-220 view on GitHub


polysim compiles part of itself (Cython) the first time it is imported. If 18 shards started at once, they would all compile at the same time into the same place. This rule does the import once, and every shard lists its marker as an input, so shards start only after the build exists. The marker stands for “a side effect has happened”, which no file output can express.


The fan-out: locus × condition × replicate × shard



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

##### Define rules #####
rule all:
    input:
        expand(f"{L('done')}/analyzeCondition_{{condition}}.done",
               locus=LOCUS_NAMES, condition=COND_NAMES),
        f"{OUT}/{RUN_NAME}_benchmarking.tsv"


ChromSimPipe, lines 160-165 view on GitHub


rule all asks for one analyzeCondition marker per locus and condition. Everything else is pulled in backwards: each condition marker needs N_REPLICATES merge markers, each merge marker needs N_SHARDS shard markers. Change n_shards from 2 to 4 and the number of GPU jobs doubles while each one saves half as many frames (frames_per_replicate is split across shards).



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

def L(key):
    """A per-locus folder as a pattern with a {locus} wildcard."""
    return f"{OUT}/loci/{{locus}}/{key}"


def LP(wildcards, key):
    """A per-locus folder for a job's locus."""
    return rel(locus_paths(wildcards.locus)[key])


ChromSimPipe, lines 73-80 view on GitHub


L() and LP() are small helpers worth copying. In L(), the f-string {locus} produces a literal {locus}, so L('done') is a pattern with a wildcard in it. That is the same escaping as MicroCPipe’s {group} inside expand(), for a different reason: here it is f-string braces, not expand() braces. LP() gives the concrete folder for a job’s locus.



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

wildcard_constraints:
    locus = r"[^/]+",
    rep   = r"\d+",
    shard = r"\d+"


ChromSimPipe, lines 94-97 view on GitHub


The constraints here are regexes, not name lists: a locus is anything without a slash, replicate and shard are digits. parameters.py refuses locus names that contain /, which is what makes [^/]+ safe.


An input function that adds an ordering



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

rule analyzeCondition:
    input:
        merged = lambda wildcards: expand(rules.mergeShards.output.done, locus=wildcards.locus,
                                          condition=wildcards.condition,
                                          rep=range(N_REPLICATES)),
        mcool  = compare_mcool,
        ## with calibration.msd.reference_condition, other conditions wait for its units
        reference = lambda wildcards: (
            [f"{OUT}/loci/{wildcards.locus}/done/analyzeCondition_{CALIBRATION['msd']['reference_condition']}.done"]
            if CALIBRATION["msd"]["reference_condition"]
            and CALIBRATION["default_anchor"] == "msd"
            and wildcards.condition != CALIBRATION["msd"]["reference_condition"] else [])
    output:
        done = f"{L('done')}/analyzeCondition_{{condition}}.done"
    log:
        err = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/analyzeCondition_{{condition}}.err",
        out = f"{LOG_DIR}/{{locus}}/analyzeCondition_{{condition}}.out"
    benchmark:
        f"{BENCH_DIR}/analyzeCondition_{{locus}}_{{condition}}.tsv"
    params:
        configfile = CONFIGFILE,
        sim_dir    = lambda wildcards: LP(wildcards, "sims"),
        out_dir    = lambda wildcards: f"{LP(wildcards, 'analysis')}/{wildcards.condition}",
        mcool_dir  = MCOOL_DIR,
        n_jobs     = ANALYSIS["n_jobs"],
        msd_flag   = "" if ANALYSIS["msd"] else "--no-msd"
    conda: ENV_SIM
    shell:
        """
        mkdir -p {params.out_dir}
        CHROMSIM_CONFIG={params.configfile} CHROMSIM_LOCUS={wildcards.locus} \
            "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python" scripts/run_analysis_all.py \
            --results-dir {params.sim_dir} \
            --output-dir {params.out_dir} \
            --condition {wildcards.condition} \
            --hic-dir {params.mcool_dir} \
            --n-jobs {params.n_jobs} \
            --skip-existing \
            {params.msd_flag} 1> {log.out} 2> {log.err}
        touch {output.done}
        """


ChromSimPipe, lines 344-384 view on GitHub


Three inputs, three input-function patterns:

merged gathers the replicates of this condition (as in mergeShards).
mcool = compare_mcool returns the converted Hi-C map for this condition, or an empty list when the condition has none. An empty list is a valid input: it just adds nothing.
reference returns another condition’s analyzeCondition marker, but only when the config asks every condition to reuse one reference condition’s calibration. This makes the rule depend on another job of the same rule, which forces an order without any file passing between them.

Note --skip-existing in the command. The script skips a replicate whose contact map already exists. Combined with markers, that means deleting analyzeCondition_<condition>.done reruns the job, but the job may then skip the work. Delete the analysis output folder too if you want it recomputed.


GPU jobs from the profile
The simulateShard rule says nothing about GPUs except --gpu 0. The request is in the profile:



profiles/slurm-template/config.yaml

simulateShard:
  runtime: 720
  slurm_partition: <gpu partition>
  gpu: 1                          # becomes --gpus=1. Prefer this: on Pioneer a
                                  # gres: "'gpu:1'" request was never submitted.
  # qos: <gpu qos>                # only if your site requires a QOS for GPUs
  cpus_per_task: 4
  mem_mb: 60000


ChromSimPipe, lines 37-44 view on GitHub


gpu: 1 is a standard resource the SLURM executor plugin turns into --gpus=1, and the comment records what did not work on one cluster (a gres request that was never submitted). The rule can always say device 0 because, on a typical SLURM setup, a job only sees the GPU it was given.
The local profile handles the laptop/workstation case differently:



profiles/local/config.yaml

## Run everything on the current machine (a workstation, or one interactive
## node with a GPU): no scheduler. Start with: bash ChromSimPipe.sh
cores: all
software-deployment-method: conda
latency-wait: 60

## Global limits: at most one simulation per GPU, and the machine's memory.
resources:
  - gpu=1
  - mem_mb=64000

set-resources:
  simulateShard:
    gpu: 1
    mem_mb: 60000
  mergeShards:
    mem_mb: 64000
  analyzeCondition:
    mem_mb: 64000


ChromSimPipe, lines 1-19 view on GitHub


resources: - gpu=1 is a global limit: the whole run has one GPU, and each simulateShard job claims it (set-resources: simulateShard: gpu: 1), so only one simulation runs at a time while other rules still run beside it. To test on a machine with no GPU, the config’s polysim: platform: CUDA can be set to CPU.
ChromSimPipe’s SLURM profiles set cpus_per_task instead of set-threads, and the rules have no threads: at all. The analysis parallelizes with analysis.n_jobs from the config, and the profile comment says to keep cpus_per_task at least that large. Two numbers in two files that must agree is the price of keeping resources out of the rules.


parameters.py: one source of truth for Snakemake and scripts



configs/parameters.py

"""
Simulation parameters loader - reads config/ChromSimConfig.yaml and the
samplesheet it names. Nothing here is hard-coded: every value comes from the
config (set CHROMSIM_CONFIG=/path/to/config.yaml to use another file).

Relative paths in the config and samplesheet are resolved against the repo
root, so one samplesheet pointing at data/... works on every cluster (each
cluster links its own files into data/). A relative outputDir is resolved
against $CHROMSIM_OUTPUT_ROOT when that is set (e.g. a scratch directory),
else against the repo root.

Several loci can be listed under `loci:`. Every value below describes ONE
active locus: $CHROMSIM_LOCUS if set (the workflow sets it for every job),
else the first locus in the config. LOCI and locus_paths() describe all of them.

Public API used by the Snakefile and scripts:

    CONFIG_PATH, REPO_ROOT, OUTPUT_ROOT, OUTPUT_DIR, PATHS, GENOME
    LOCI, LOCUS_NAMES, ACTIVE_LOCUS, locus_paths(), locus_tiling()
    CHROM, REGION_START, REGION_END, RESOLUTION, N_MONOMERS
    TILING, SIM_RUN, POLYSIM, N_REPLICATES, N_SHARDS
    SAMPLES, SIMULATION_CONDITIONS, ALL_PARAM_SETS
    GENOME_ASSEMBLY, CTCF_TYPES, CTCF_PEAKS, CTCF_BEDS, CTCF_SITES_BY_TYPE
    HIC_TYPES, HIC_FILES, MCOOL_FILES
    get_condition(), list_conditions()
    get_ctcf_arrays(), load_ctcf_from_bed()
    get_tiled_ctcf_arrays(), get_msd_pairs()
    ANALYSIS, DATA, MSD_PROBE, MSD_FIT, CALIBRATION

Sample names are built from the samplesheet columns listed in
``fileNamesFrom``; conditions refer to samples by that name.
"""


ChromSimPipe, lines 1-32 view on GitHub


In MicroCPipe and TTpipe, the Snakefile reads the config and passes values to scripts on the command line. ChromSimPipe has dozens of physics parameters, and the simulation and analysis scripts need most of them. Instead of passing them all as arguments, everything reads one module:



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

##### Load config and sample sheets #####
## `--configfile other.yaml` replaces the default config entirely (it must be
## a complete config); configs/parameters.py reads the same file, here and in
## every job, via $CHROMSIM_CONFIG. Each per-locus job also gets $CHROMSIM_LOCUS.
DEFAULT_CONFIG = "config/ChromSimConfig.yaml"
if not workflow.overwrite_configfiles:
    configfile: DEFAULT_CONFIG
CONFIGFILE = os.path.abspath((list(workflow.overwrite_configfiles) or [DEFAULT_CONFIG])[-1])
os.environ["CHROMSIM_CONFIG"] = CONFIGFILE

sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())
from configs.parameters import (
    SIMULATION_CONDITIONS, CTCF_TYPES, CTCF_PEAKS, HIC_FILES, MCOOL_FILES,
    SAMPLES, RUN_NAME, N_REPLICATES, N_SHARDS, ANALYSIS, CALIBRATION, GENOME_ASSEMBLY, GENOME,
    OUTPUT_DIR, LOCI, LOCUS_NAMES, locus_paths, ctcf_bed_path, condition_peak_files,
)


ChromSimPipe, lines 29-44 view on GitHub



Lines 33-35: the Snakefile loads the default config only if no --configfile was given. Normally Snakemake merges a configfile: in the Snakefile with --configfile on the command line. Here the author wanted the command-line file to replace the default completely, because the scripts read one file.
Lines 36-37: the chosen file’s absolute path goes into $CHROMSIM_CONFIG.
Lines 39-44: the Snakefile imports configs.parameters, which reads $CHROMSIM_CONFIG itself.
The per-locus rules set CHROMSIM_CONFIG and CHROMSIM_LOCUS in front of the script call (see simulateShard above), so each script imports the same module and sees the values for its own locus.

The module also validates more than either other pipeline does, with messages that say how to fix the problem:



configs/parameters.py

try:
    _start, _end = int(_l["region_start"]), int(_l["region_end"])
except (TypeError, ValueError):
    raise ValueError(f"Locus {_name}: region_start and region_end must be whole numbers "
                     f"in bp (e.g. 64210000, not 64.21Mb or 64,210,000)") from None
if _start < 0 or _end <= _start:
    raise ValueError(f"Locus {_name}: need 0 <= region_start < region_end (got {_start}-{_end})")
if _start % RESOLUTION or _end % RESOLUTION:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Locus {_name}: region_start and region_end must be multiples of resolution "
        f"({RESOLUTION} bp) so each simulated monomer lines up with one Hi-C bin; "
        f"e.g. {_start // RESOLUTION * RESOLUTION}-{-(-_end // RESOLUTION) * RESOLUTION}")


ChromSimPipe, lines 107-118 view on GitHub


The trade-off is that Snakemake no longer sees the values. Two consequences:

Changing a physics parameter does not rerun anything. simulateShard passes only the config file’s path as a param, so Snakemake’s params rerun trigger sees no change, and the config file is not an input. The repository’s troubleshooting table says it plainly: “Parameter changed but nothing reruns … delete the markers for the steps to redo”.
--config key=value does not reach the scripts. It changes Snakemake’s config dictionary, which the Snakefile uses for a few things (resolution, the motif, the conda envs), while parameters.py and every script read the file. --config n_shards=4 changes nothing, quietly.



A parse-time write that respects the cluster



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

## Write the parsed samplesheet (with sample names) next to the outputs.
## Only rewritten when it changes: every cluster job re-parses this file.
_sheet = f"{OUT}/{RUN_NAME}_ChromSimSamplesheet.txt"
_cols  = list(next(iter(SAMPLES.values()))["metadata"])
_text  = "\t".join(["sampleName"] + _cols) + "\n" + "".join(
    "\t".join([name] + [s["metadata"][c] for c in _cols]) + "\n"
    for name, s in SAMPLES.items()
)
if not os.path.exists(_sheet) or open(_sheet).read() != _text:
    os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
    with open(_sheet, "w") as _fh:
        _fh.write(_text)


ChromSimPipe, lines 99-110 view on GitHub


The Snakefile writes a copy of the parsed samplesheet next to the outputs. The comment points at a detail most people learn the hard way: on a cluster, every job parses the Snakefile again. An unconditional write would rewrite the file from every job at once. Comparing first means it is written once. (It also means snakemake --lint and -n write this file; parse-time code always runs.)


Conda environments: a file, a name or a path



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

def conda_env(key):
    """Resolve a condaEnvs entry: an env file, an existing env name, or an env path."""
    env = os.path.expanduser(str(config["condaEnvs"][key]))
    if env.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")) and not os.path.isabs(env):
        return os.path.abspath(env)   # Snakemake resolves env files from workflows/ otherwise
    return env


ChromSimPipe, lines 55-60 view on GitHub


conda: accepts an environment file, or the name or path of an existing environment. The config allows all three, so a cluster where building the GPU environment is slow can point at one built by hand. The abspath line handles a quirk: a relative .yml path in conda: is resolved from the Snakefile’s folder (workflows/), not from the repository root.


A rule that exists only if needed



workflows/ChromSimPipe.snakefile

if not MOTIF.get("meme"):
    rule getMotif:
        output:
            meme = MOTIF_MEME
        log:
            err = f"{LOG_DIR}/getMotif_{MOTIF['jaspar_id']}.err",
            out = f"{LOG_DIR}/getMotif_{MOTIF['jaspar_id']}.out"
        benchmark:
            f"{BENCH_DIR}/getMotif_{MOTIF['jaspar_id']}.tsv"
        params:
            url = MOTIF["jaspar_url"].format(jaspar_id=MOTIF["jaspar_id"])
        conda: ENV_CTCF
        shell:
            """
            wget -O {output.meme} "{params.url}" 1> {log.out} 2> {log.err}
            grep -q "^MOTIF" {output.meme} || {{ echo "Not a MEME file: {params.url}" >> {log.err}; exit 1; }}
            """


ChromSimPipe, lines 188-204 view on GitHub


Same pattern as TTpipe’s if TRIM:. With a local MEME file in the config, there is no download rule, and MOTIF_MEME points at the local file, which then has to exist. The shell block checks that the download is really a MEME file, with the || {{ ...; exit 1; }} form from module 4, because a web server can return an error page with status 200.


Testing
ChromSimPipe’s tests are unit tests: tests/test_parameters_config.py, test_loci.py and test_paths.py import parameters.py with small temporary configs and check paths, loci and validation messages. There is no dry-run test and no CI workflow for the tests (the only workflow publishes the docs). The test config is the substitute: one GPU job end to end, run by hand on a new cluster.

text:
What you would change

Put the condition’s parameters into params:. For example params: cond = lambda w: COND_LOOKUP[w.condition] in simulateShard. Snakemake stores params and reruns a job when they change, so editing ctcf_capture would rerun that condition’s shards and everything after them, without anyone deleting markers.
Add a dry-run fixture and a CI job. A tiny samplesheet and config under tests/, as in MicroCPipe and TTpipe, would let a dry run assert the 10-job and 39-job counts. 
Declare the merged folder as directory(). Its name is known in the Snakefile (merged_<params_name>_ctcf-<ctcf_type>_rep<N>, all from COND_LOOKUP), so mergeShards could declare it and Snakemake would clear it before a rerun.
Make getMotif a local rule (localrules: getMotif). It downloads from the internet, and compute nodes on some clusters have no outside network.
Keep account names out of shipped profiles. profiles/longleaf and profiles/pioneer carry real SLURM accounts; the other two pipelines ship <account> placeholders and a launcher check.

title: ChromSimPipe
text:
Exercises for the curious

Add a second locus to loci:. How many more jobs does a full run have, and which jobs are not repeated?
You lower ctcf_capture for cond2_weak-ctcf and resubmit. What runs? What would you delete to get the right result today?
Rewrite mergeShards to declare its merged folder with directory() instead of a marker. What do you gain, and what new problem appears for analyzeCondition?
Why does preparePolysim not need a {locus} wildcard, while validateCTCF does?







NoteShort answers






Per locus: 2 orientCTCF (one per CTCF sample), 1 validateCTCF, 18 simulateShard, 9 mergeShards, 3 analyzeCondition, so 33 more jobs.  convertHic, getMotif, preparePolysim and benchmarkSummary are shared and still run once.
Nothing reruns: the markers exist, and nothing Snakemake tracks changed. Delete the simulateShard_cond2_weak-ctcf_*, mergeShards_cond2_weak-ctcf_* and analyzeCondition_cond2_weak-ctcf.done markers for that locus, and that condition’s analysis folder (because of --skip-existing), then resubmit.
Snakemake now knows the merged data exists, clears it before a rerun, and --summary reports it. But analyzeCondition reads the merged folders through --results-dir (the whole sims/ folder), so you would also want its input to name those folders, or the dependency is only on paper. The shard folders would still need markers unless you give them the same treatment.
The polysim build is the same for every locus, so it runs once. validateCTCF checks the CTCF sites inside one locus window, which differ per locus.




Next: how our pipelines compare to community conventions

title: TTpipe
text:
TTpipe is the largest of the three pipelines: seven rule files plus common.smk, 33 rule definitions (a few are two variants of one rule), and a config with switches that turn whole halves of the workflow on and off. It is the place to see module 6 (structure) and module 8 (testing) at full size.
Code on this page is pulled from the repository at the pinned commit (ebdc210), and each block links to the same lines on GitHub. Line numbers in the text are the file’s own line numbers.

title: TTpipe
text:
What the pipeline does
TT-seq measures transcription as it happens. Cells are given 4-thiouridine (4sU) for a short pulse, so only RNA made during those minutes carries the label. The labeled RNA is fragmented and pulled down, and the library is sequenced strand-specifically. Because most of that RNA is freshly made and not yet spliced, reads cover introns as well as exons, and the signal reflects how much polymerase passed through a gene during the pulse rather than how much mature RNA has piled up. TTpipe reimplements the TT-seq workflow described for Magnitov et al. 2024 (Mol Cell, GEO GSE260914); the shipped samplesheet describes that study’s eight mouse ES cell samples (ZFP143 degradation: DMSO, 2 h, 6 h, 24 h, two replicates each), with paths you replace.
Processing aligns read pairs with STAR, keeps reads with MAPQ ≥ 10, removes PCR duplicates with Picard, and splits each BAM into the two genomic strands. Replicates of a condition are merged and turned into scaled bigWig tracks, and HTSeq counts reads over whole gene bodies on each strand. Analysis runs DESeq2 for every comparison against a reference condition, ranks genes for preranked GSEA (fgsea), and draws a Sankey diagram of how genes move between up, down and unchanged across the comparisons. Reports summarize QC, strandedness and replicate agreement.

title: TTpipe
text:
The rule graph



The graph has two halves joined at the count matrix. Processing runs from fastqc and star_align down to bigwig and count_matrix; analysis runs from count_matrix (or a matrix you supply) and sample_table through deseq2, rnk, fgsea and sankey. The report rules (qc_summary, qc_report, multiqc, results_explorer, stranded_signal) hang off both. Which boxes exist depends on the config: with trim: true there is a fastp box, with gsea_collections set there are rnk and fgsea boxes, and with run_processing: false the whole top half is gone.
The repository keeps its own diagrams in docs/img/, and tests/test_dag.py fails when they no longer match snakemake --rulegraph, so they cannot drift from the code.
On the test fixture (2 conditions × 2 replicates) the full dry run plans 60 jobs, among them 4 star_align, 8 fastqc (two mates × four samples), 8 split_strands and 8 htseq_count (two strands × four samples), and 6 bigwig (two conditions × all/forward/reverse).

title: TTpipe
section: A walk from inputs to outputs
text:
A walk from inputs to outputs

samplesheet.txt: one row per sample with Name, Condition, Replicate, and the FASTQ columns (only needed when processing runs).
config/TTpipeConfig.yaml: the switches (run_processing, run_analysis, qc_report, trim, multiqc, spike_in), the reference, strandedness, and the DESeq2/GSEA settings.
workflows/rules/common.smk reads both, checks them, and defines every output path as a template plus the target functions.
Per sample: fastqc → (fastp) → star_align → mapq_filter → mark_duplicates → split_strands → htseq_count.
Per condition: merge_bams → scale_factors → bigwig.
Once: gene_info, count_matrix, sample_table, deseq2, sankey, the reports.
Per comparison and gene-set collection: rnk → fgsea.

text:
Concepts in the wild

The samplesheet as an input
This is the most instructive rule in the three pipelines, because it records a bug that happened.



workflows/TTpipe.snakefile

## Sample metadata for DESeq2 (and the report), straight from the samplesheet.
## The samplesheet is an input so that editing it (adding samples, changing conditions) regenerates this table;
## without it Snakemake would keep a stale table from an earlier run (seen on a real run: DESeq2 then failed
## with 'sample names differ between the count matrix and the sample table').
rule sample_table:
    input:
        config["samplesheet"],
    output:
        SAMPLES_DESEQ2,
    run:
        import os
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(output[0]), exist_ok=True)
        with open(output[0], "w") as fh:
            fh.write("sample\tcondition\treplicate\n")
            for s in SAMPLES:
                fh.write(f"{s}\t{SAMPLE_TABLE.loc[s, 'Condition']}\t{SAMPLE_TABLE.loc[s, 'Replicate']}\n")


TTpipe, lines 35-50 view on GitHub


sample_table writes the sample/condition/replicate table DESeq2 reads. The run: block takes the values from SAMPLES and SAMPLE_TABLE, which common.smk built from the samplesheet when the Snakefile was parsed. So the rule does not need to read the samplesheet. It lists it as input anyway, and the comment says why: without it, adding samples to the sheet did not rerun the rule. The output already existed and none of its inputs had changed, so Snakemake kept the old table, and DESeq2 then failed because the count matrix and the table listed different samples.
The lesson for module 7: Snakemake reruns a job when something it tracks changes. Python values computed at parse time are not tracked. If a rule’s output depends on a file, put the file in input:, even when the rule gets the values some other way. qc_summary and qc_report do the same, and tests/test_stale_inputs.py checks it by really running the rule, appending two samples, and running it again:



tests/test_stale_inputs.py

def test_sample_table_follows_the_samplesheet(tmp_path):
    sheet = tmp_path / "samplesheet.txt"
    shutil.copy(ROOT / "tests/dryrun/samplesheet.txt", sheet)
    out = tmp_path / "out"
    target = out / "counts" / "samples_deseq2.txt"

    r = run([str(target)], out, sheet)
    assert r.returncode == 0, r.stderr
    assert len(target.read_text().splitlines()) == 1 + 4          # header + 4 samples

    # unchanged samplesheet: nothing to redo
    r = run(["-n", str(target)], out, sheet)
    assert "Nothing to be done" in (r.stdout + r.stderr)

    # add two samples (a new condition); wait so the samplesheet's mtime is newer than the table's
    time.sleep(1.5)
    with open(sheet, "a") as fh:
        fh.write("CI_6H_rep1\t6H\trep1\tR1.fastq.gz\tR2.fastq.gz\ttests/dryrun/\n")
        fh.write("CI_6H_rep2\t6H\trep2\tR1.fastq.gz\tR2.fastq.gz\ttests/dryrun/\n")

    r = run([str(target)], out, sheet)
    assert r.returncode == 0, r.stderr
    rows = target.read_text().splitlines()
    assert len(rows) == 1 + 6
    assert any(line.startswith("CI_6H_rep2\t6H\trep2") for line in rows)

RUN_ANALYSIS = bool(config.get("run_analysis", True))
RUN_REPORT = bool(config.get("qc_report", True))

Three booleans decide which parts of the workflow exist. Note the guard right after them: a config with every switch off is an error, not a run that does nothing. The two string settings are checked against their allowed values immediately, so strandedness: dUTp fails at parse time with the allowed values in the message.
The Snakefile then includes rule files, one of them only when a switch is on:

TRIM = bool(config.get("trim", False))
PY = "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python"

                     "or set build_star_index: true to build one")


def raw_reads(w):
    return [SAMPLE_TABLE.loc[w.sample, "R1"], SAMPLE_TABLE.loc[w.sample, "R2"]]


def star_reads(w):
    """Trimmed reads when trim is true, raw FASTQs otherwise."""
    if TRIM:
        return [TRIM_R.format(sample=w.sample, mate=m) for m in ("1", "2")]

## Optional adapter / quality trimming (not in the guide; config trim: true). fastp defaults

if TRIM:

        input:

        output:
            r1 = temp(TRIM_R.replace("{mate}", "1")),
            r2 = temp(TRIM_R.replace("{mate}", "2")),

When trim is false, there is no fastp rule at all, and star_reads() hands STAR the raw FASTQs. When it is true, star_reads() returns the trimmed paths, which only fastp can produce, so the DAG gains one fastp job per sample. The test test_trim_adds_fastp checks exactly that: four more jobs, all of them fastp.
Two small things in fastp: TRIM_R.replace("{mate}", "1") fills in one wildcard of a template by hand and leaves {sample} for Snakemake, and both trimmed files are temp(), removed once STAR has read them.
The same trick gives variants of a rule. processing.smk defines scale_factors, bigwig_sample and count_matrix under if not SPIKE_ENABLED:, and spike.smk defines rules with the same names for the spike-in case. Exactly one version exists in any run. Profiles key on rule names, so one set-resources: scale_factors: entry covers both.

## Condition bigWig factors. 'tracks' in spike_in.normalize: max(spike-in pairs) / this condition's (source
## 'spike-in'). Otherwise the usual library-size factor, but on host pairs only (the spike-in reads would
## otherwise count as library). config scale_factors still overrides a condition.
rule scale_factors:
    input:
        counts = SPIKE_COUNTS,
    output:
        table = SCALE_FACTORS,
    log:
        OUT + "/logs/scale_factors.log",
    benchmark:
        OUT + "/benchmarks/scale_factors.tsv",
    threads: 1
    params:

        basis = "spike" if SPIKE_TRACKS else "host",
        order = " ".join(CONDITIONS),
        overrides = " ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in (config.get("scale_factors") or {}).items()),
    shell:

        {PY} {params.script} --spike-counts {input.counts} --group-by condition --basis {params.basis} \
            --order {params.order} --override {params.overrides} --out {output.table} 2> {log}
        """

Compare its input (the spike-in counts table) with the plain version’s (the merged BAMs). The two variants need different inputs, which is why this is two rules and not one rule with an if inside params.


Target functions
rule all in TTpipe is one line: all_targets(). The work is in common.smk:



workflows/rules/common.smk

def processing_targets():
    t = []
    t += expand(FASTQC_ZIP, sample=SAMPLES, mate=["1", "2"])
    t += expand(BAI, sample=SAMPLES)
    t += expand(STRAND_BAI, sample=SAMPLES, strand=STRANDS)
    t += expand(BIGWIG, condition=CONDITIONS)
    t += expand(BIGWIG_STRAND, condition=CONDITIONS, strand=STRANDS)
    if config.get("sample_tracks", False):
        t += expand(SAMPLE_BIGWIG, sample=SAMPLES)
        t += expand(SAMPLE_BIGWIG_STRAND, sample=SAMPLES, strand=STRANDS)
    t += [COUNTS_FORWARD, COUNTS_REVERSE, COUNTS_DESEQ2, GENE_INFO, SCALE_FACTORS]
    if SPIKE_ENABLED:
        t += [SPIKE_COUNTS, SPIKE_CONTIG_COUNTS, SPIKE_CONTIGS]
        if SPIKE_SRC_GTF:
            t.append(COUNTS_SPIKE)
    return t


TTpipe, lines 326-341 view on GitHub





workflows/rules/common.smk

def stranded_targets():
    """The stranded signal page, when `stranded_plots` is true (default) AND the stranded bigWigs are made in this run
    or already exist (an analysis-only run on an output folder that was processed earlier). Without bigWigs the page is
    skipped quietly: an analysis-only run on a count matrix has nothing to draw."""
    if not config.get("stranded_plots", True):
        return []
    if RUN_PROCESSING:
        return [STRANDED_SIGNAL]
    if RUN_ANALYSIS:
        needed = (expand(BIGWIG_STRAND, condition=CONDITIONS, strand=STRANDS)
                  + [SCALE_FACTORS, GENE_INFO, COUNTS_FORWARD, COUNTS_REVERSE])
        if all(os.path.exists(f) for f in needed):
            return [STRANDED_SIGNAL]
    return []


def report_targets():
    return [QC_REPORT]


def all_targets():
    t = []
    if RUN_PROCESSING:
        t += processing_targets()
    if RUN_ANALYSIS:
        t += analysis_targets()
    t += stranded_targets()
    if RUN_REPORT:
        t += report_targets()
    if RUN_PROCESSING and config.get("multiqc", False):
        t.append(MULTIQC_REPORT)
    return t


TTpipe, lines 356-387 view on GitHub



Each part of the workflow has its own function, and all_targets() adds them up according to the switches.
Every path is built from a template defined once near the top of common.smk (FASTQC_ZIP, BIGWIG_STRAND, …). The rules use the same templates as their outputs, so the target list and the rules cannot disagree about a filename.
stranded_targets() is the subtle one. In an analysis-only run, the stranded bigWigs are not built in this run. The page is requested only if the files already exist on disk from an earlier run; otherwise it is skipped quietly. That is a target function deciding based on the file system at parse time, which is fine for targets but would be a mistake inside a rule’s inputs.

Same idea as MicroCPipe: each wildcard matches only the real names. The or "NONE" matters when the list is empty (no GSEA collections): "|".join([]) is the empty string, an empty pattern that matches an empty wildcard value. "NONE" keeps the constraint a real pattern that no file uses.
merge_bams uses a rule-level constraint to let one rule make three files per condition:



workflows/rules/processing.smk

##### Tracks #####
## Replicates of a condition merged: all reads (suffix '') and per strand (suffix '_forward' / '_reverse').
## Output names equal MERGED_BAM / MERGED_STRAND_BAM; one rule serves both. Merged BAMs are for tracks only.
## Inputs are sorted, so the merge is sorted (guide sorts again; same result).
rule merge_bams:
    input:
        bams = lambda w: [(BAM.format(sample=s) if w.suffix == "" else
                           STRAND_BAM.format(sample=s, strand=w.suffix[1:]))
                          for s in SAMPLES_BY_CONDITION[w.condition]],
    output:
        bam = OUT + "/merged/{condition}{suffix}.bam",
        bai = OUT + "/merged/{condition}{suffix}.bam.bai",
    wildcard_constraints:
        suffix = "|_forward|_reverse",
    log:
        OUT + "/logs/merge_bams_{condition}{suffix}.log",
    benchmark:
        OUT + "/benchmarks/merge_bams_{condition}{suffix}.tsv",
    threads: 8
    conda: ENVS + "/ttpipe_tracks.yml"
    shell:
        """
        if [ $(echo {input.bams} | wc -w) -eq 1 ]; then
            cp {input.bams} {output.bam} 2> {log}
        else
            samtools merge -@ {threads} -f {output.bam} {input.bams} 2> {log}
        fi
        samtools index -@ {threads} {output.bam} 2>> {log}
        """

suffix = "|_forward|_reverse" allows the empty string as one of the alternatives, so merged/DMSO.bam, merged/DMSO_forward.bam and merged/DMSO_reverse.bam all come from this rule. By default a wildcard has to match at least one character, so without the constraint the all-reads BAM would have no rule. The input lambda then picks the right per-sample BAMs from the suffix.


Shell escaping in the real world

## Scale factor per condition = (largest mapped read-pair count) / (this one's), on the merged all-reads
## BAMs, pairs = records / 2 (guide). config scale_factors overrides a condition (source 'config').
## The maximum is taken over all conditions, including overridden ones.
if not SPIKE_ENABLED:   # the spike-in variants of this rule are in rules/spike.smk
    rule scale_factors:
        input:
            bams = expand(OUT + "/merged/{condition}.bam", condition=CONDITIONS),
        output:
            table = SCALE_FACTORS,
        log:
            OUT + "/logs/scale_factors.log",
        benchmark:
            OUT + "/benchmarks/scale_factors.tsv",
        threads: 1
        conda: ENVS + "/ttpipe_tracks.yml"
        params:
            cond_bams = " ".join(f"{c}={OUT}/merged/{c}.bam" for c in CONDITIONS),
            overrides = " ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in (config.get("scale_factors") or {}).items()),
            script = SCRIPTS + "/scale_factors.py",
            tmp = OUT + "/tracks/scale_factors_pairs.tmp",
        shell:
            """
        : > {params.tmp}
        for kv in {params.cond_bams}; do
            c=${{kv%%=*}}; b=${{kv#*=}}
            n=$(samtools view -@ {threads} -c "$b")
            printf '%s\\t%s\\n' "$c" $((n / 2)) >> {params.tmp}
        done

## bamCoverage --scaleFactor SF -p threads -b BAM -o BW (guide; no other normalization).
## --binSize is passed explicitly (default 50 = deepTools' own default, so the same as the guide).
rule bigwig:
    input:
        bam = OUT + "/merged/{condition}{suffix}.bam",
        bai = OUT + "/merged/{condition}{suffix}.bam.bai",
        sf = SCALE_FACTORS,
    output:
        bw = OUT + "/tracks/{condition}{suffix}.bw",
    wildcard_constraints:
        suffix = "|_forward|_reverse",
    log:
        OUT + "/logs/bigwig_{condition}{suffix}.log",
    benchmark:
        OUT + "/benchmarks/bigwig_{condition}{suffix}.tsv",
    threads: 8
    conda: ENVS + "/ttpipe_tracks.yml"
    params:
        bin = config.get("bigwig_bin_size", 50),
        extra = config.get("bigwig_extra", ""),
    shell:
        """
        SF=$(awk -F'\\t' -v c={wildcards.condition} '$1==c {{print $3}}' {input.sf})
        [ -n "$SF" ] || {{ echo "no scale factor for {wildcards.condition}" > {log}; exit 1; }}
        bamCoverage --scaleFactor $SF -p {threads} -b {input.bam} -o {output.bw} \
            --binSize {params.bin} {params.extra} > {log} 2>&1
        """


TTpipe, lines 303-329 view on GitHub


Three escapes from module 4 in a few lines:

${{kv%%=*}} is bash’s ${kv%%=*} (everything before the first =) with the braces doubled so Snakemake leaves them alone.
awk ... '$1==c {{print $3}}' is the same rule for awk’s braces.
'%s\\t%s\\n' is written with two backslashes so the shell script contains \t, which printf turns into a tab. MicroCPipe’s preseq fallback writes a single \t, so Python puts a literal tab character in the script; both work, but the doubled form keeps the command readable in -p output.

The [ -n "$SF" ] || { ...; exit 1; } line in bigwig is the opposite of MicroCPipe’s preseq fallback: here an empty scale factor is a real error, so the block writes a message and fails the job on purpose.
{PY} in these commands is not a rule field. It is the module-level variable PY = "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python" from the top of processing.smk; Snakemake fills shell placeholders from the rule’s fields first and then from global variables. It works, but the linter flags it (see conventions), and a reader looking for PY in the rule will not find it.

deseq2 runs once for all comparisons and writes one CSV per comparison. The R script needs the pattern degs_{comparison}.csv, with the braces still in it, to know where to write. A plain string param would be formatted with the job’s wildcards and fail (this rule has no {comparison} wildcard). Wrapping it in lambda wildcards: DEGS turns that off: Snakemake does not format the value a params function returns.
The neighboring rule shows a constraint from module 2 that is easy to forget:



workflows/rules/analysis.smk

## Ranked list (symbol <TAB> Wald stat). RNK has no {collection} wildcard, so it cannot be a second
## output of the per-collection fgsea rule (Snakemake requires equal wildcards in all outputs): own rule.
rule rnk:
    input:
        degs = DEGS,
        gene_info = GENE_INFO,
    output:

def qc_summary_inputs(wildcards):
    # the samplesheet is listed so that editing it reruns the summary (it is read via --samplesheet)
    return [config["samplesheet"]] + _qc_summary_data_inputs(wildcards)


def _qc_summary_data_inputs(wildcards):
    if RUN_PROCESSING:
        return (expand(STAR_LOG, sample=SAMPLES) + expand(STAR_GENECNT, sample=SAMPLES)
                + expand(MAPQ_STATS, sample=SAMPLES) + expand(DEDUP_METRICS, sample=SAMPLES)
                + expand(FINAL_STATS, sample=SAMPLES)
                + [COUNTS_FORWARD, COUNTS_REVERSE, COUNTS_DESEQ2, GENE_INFO])
    if RUN_ANALYSIS:
        # analysis-only: only the count matrix (+ gene table, which the analysis needs anyway)
        return [QC_COUNTS, GENE_INFO]
    # report-only run: use whatever already exists on disk, nothing is built
    return [p for p in [QC_COUNTS, GENE_INFO] if os.path.exists(p)]


def qc_report_inputs(wildcards):
    d = {"sample_qc": SAMPLE_QC, "samplesheet": config["samplesheet"]}
    if RUN_ANALYSIS:
        d["deg"] = DEG_SUMMARY
        d["vst"] = VST_COUNTS
    if RUN_PROCESSING:
        d["scale"] = SCALE_FACTORS
        d["bigwigs"] = expand(BIGWIG, condition=CONDITIONS) + expand(BIGWIG_STRAND, condition=CONDITIONS, strand=STRANDS)
        if config.get("sample_tracks", False):
            d["bigwigs"] += expand(SAMPLE_BIGWIG, sample=SAMPLES) + expand(SAMPLE_BIGWIG_STRAND, sample=SAMPLES, strand=STRANDS)
    return d

The QC report reads different files in a processing-only, analysis-only or full run. Its input function returns a dictionary, and qc_report uses unpack(qc_report_inputs) so each key becomes a named input ({input.sample_qc}, {input.scale}). In a report-only run, _qc_summary_data_inputs lists only files that already exist, so nothing is built.


Resources in profiles, and one launcher difference
The resource story is MicroCPipe’s: rules declare only threads:, and every rule has a set-threads and set-resources entry in each profile. The local profile’s comments are honest about where the numbers come from:

TTpipe’s launcher activates the venv, the thing MicroCPipe’s launcher deliberately avoids. TTpipe copes on the inside instead: every script is run as $CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python (PY in processing.smk), and the comments in report.smk say why (“the launcher’s venv bin/ is first on PATH in cluster jobs”). Python tools inside the conda environments can still hit the problem MicroCPipe describes when an environment path is long enough for conda to rewrite their first line. Two other differences from MicroCPipe: TTpipe’s SLURM profiles have no cores: 100 line, and the launcher has no check for unedited <placeholder> values. If you run TTpipe on SLURM, check a star_align log for the thread count it actually used.

def dry_run(*configs, **kv):
    """Dry run with the main config overlaid by `configs`; kv become --config key=value (use 'True'/'False')."""
    cmd = [SNAKEMAKE, "-n", "-s", "workflows/TTpipe.snakefile", "--cores", "1", "--configfile", MAIN, *configs]
    if kv:
        cmd += ["--config", *[f"{k}={v}" for k, v in kv.items()]]
    return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, text=True)


def jobs(r):
    """Rule -> job count from the first 'Job stats' table of a dry run."""
    out, started = {}, False
    for ln in r.stdout.splitlines():
        if ln.startswith("Job stats"):
            started = True
            continue
        if started:
            p = ln.split()
            if len(p) == 2 and p[1].isdigit():
                out[p[0]] = int(p[1])
            elif not ln.strip() and out:
                break
    return out

These tests check differences: turning on trim adds exactly four jobs and all of them are fastp; per-sample tracks add twelve bigwig_sample jobs; turning off the report removes exactly two. Exercises for the curious

Delete config["samplesheet"] from the input of sample_table, run the pipeline, add two samples, and run it again. What happens, and which rule fails?

The tests count jobs from snakemake -n. Name one kind of bug these tests cannot catch.







NoteShort answers






The config (a switch, off by default); common.smk (an output template and a line in processing_targets() behind the switch); a rule in processing.smk (with conda: and threads:); an env file in envs/ if no existing one has RSeQC; a set-threads/set-resources entry in every profile; a dry-run test that the switch adds one job per sample; and the docs. If the QC report should show it, report.smk and qc_report.py too.
sample_table does not rerun, because its output exists and nothing it tracks has changed. The count matrix is rebuilt (its inputs changed), so deseq2 gets a matrix with six samples and a table with four, and fails with “sample names differ between the count matrix and the sample table”. That is the bug the comment describes.
The two versions need different inputs (merged BAMs, or the spike-in counts table), and inputs decide the DAG. A single rule would need an input function that switches, plus params that switch, plus a shell command that switches. Two small rules are easier to read and to test, and because they share a name the profiles need no change.
Anything that happens when a tool runs: wrong flags, a wrong samtools -f strand mask, a script that crashes on real data. A dry run never executes a command. The unit tests in tests/ (test_processing_scripts.py, test_stranded_signal.py, …) cover some scripts on small synthetic inputs; the tools themselves were checked on real data on the cluster (docs/validation.qmd).
